faq.a: The low‑resistance shunt forces large volumes of blood back to the heart, increasing preload and cardiac output until the heart cannot compensate.
faq.q: Why does an AVM cause high‑output cardiac failure?

faq.a: Spontaneous regression is rare; most lesions persist or enlarge, so monitoring is essential.
faq.q: Can an AVM regress without treatment?

faq.a: No. Small, asymptomatic lesions may be observed; embolisation alone can be curative for selected cases.

exam: What bedside findings would make you suspect an AVM in a child with a pulsatile forearm mass? — Look for a palpable thrill, audible bruit, warm skin, and Doppler evidence of arterial flow with early venous pulsation.

A 7‑year‑old presents with new seizures and a scalp swelling. Which imaging sequence is most appropriate and why? — Obtain MRI with MR‑angiography to delineate intracranial nidus and feeding vessels; it is non‑ionising and widely available in referral centres.
How does the Schobinger staging guide urgent management? — Stage III/IV indicates bleeding, ulceration or cardiac failure, prompting rapid referral for embolisation or surgery.
Why is systemic anticoagulation contraindicated in an acute bleeding AVM? — It worsens the high‑flow shunt’s tendency to bleed and does not address the underlying vascular defect.

In a low‑resource hospital without DSA, how would you plan treatment for a symptomatic cutaneous AVM? — Use duplex ultrasound to map feeding arteries, control infection, give propranolol to reduce flow, and arrange referral for embolisation when possible.

What distinguishes an AVM from a simple arteriovenous fistula on imaging? — An AVM shows a nidus of multiple tangled vessels with early venous drainage; a fistula shows a single direct connection without a nidus.

A child with hepatic AVM develops tachycardia and hepatomegaly. What is the pathophysiological explanation and immediate management? — The shunt creates high‑output failure; manage with diuretics, beta‑blockers, and urgent referral for embolisation.

Which genetic syndrome should you screen for in a child with limb overgrowth, port‑wine stain and AVM? — Klippel‑Trenaunay syndrome; assess for underlying venous malformations and consider MRI of the limb.
ai.title: Arteriovenous Malformation (Paediatric)
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Congenital vascular lesions that create direct artery‑to‑vein connections without a capillary bed. In children they may present with bleeding, high‑output cardiac failure or neurological deficits, and require staged assessment and multidisciplinary care.

b: Nidus: core of tangled vessels
Early venous filling on angiography
No intervening capillary bed
sections.p: An arteriovenous malformation is a tangle of dysplastic vessels that shunt arterial blood directly into veins, bypassing the capillary network. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging that demonstrates a nidus of tangled vessels with early venous drainage.

t.b: Is there a high‑velocity, low‑resistance arterial signal and early venous pulsation? – Confirms superficial AVM when CT/MRI unavailable.
What is the size, location and feeding vessels? – Provides anatomy for staging and planning.
What is the exact nidus architecture? – Gold standard; guides embolisation if available.

b: Schobinger Stage I – Quiescent (warmth, bruit)
Stage II – Expansion (pain, swelling, skin changes)
Stage III – Destruction (ulceration, bleeding)
Stage IV – Decompensation (high‑output cardiac failure)
sections.p: The Spetzler‑Martin grading system (used for intracranial AVM) and the Schobinger clinical stages (cutaneous/soft‑tissue AVM) are most useful.

t.b: Which Schobinger stage is the patient in? – Determines urgency of referral and need for embolisation or surgery.

b: Congenital somatic mutation in RASA1 or ENG (most common)
Trauma or iatrogenic injury (rare)
Infection‑driven angiogenesis (e.g., chronic bacterial skin infection, schistosomiasis in hepatic AVM)
Associated syndromes: Klippel‑Trenaunay, Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia
sections.p: Most AVMs are sporadic congenital malformations. In low‑resource settings, secondary factors such as infection‑related angiogenesis or trauma can exacerbate them.

b: Pulsatile swelling with audible bruit
Recurrent bleeding or ulceration
Seizures or focal neurological signs (intracranial)
Tachycardia, bounding pulses, hepatomegaly (hepatic)
sections.p: Presentation varies by location. Cutaneous AVM shows a pulsatile mass, bruit, and warm skin. Intracranial AVM may cause seizures, focal deficits, or hemorrhage. Hepatic AVM can lead to high‑output cardiac failure.
Select tests that answer the clinical question; if advanced imaging is unavailable, rely on bedside tools and referral pathways.

t.b: Is there arterial flow within the lesion and early venous pulsation? – Confirms shunt when CTA/MRA not accessible.
Is there cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion? – Screens for high‑output failure.
Are there anaemia or coagulopathy that need correction before intervention? – Guides peri‑procedural planning.

b: Rapid expansion with skin breakdown (risk of massive bleed)
Intracranial hemorrhage (sudden headache, loss of consciousness)
High‑output cardiac failure (dyspnoea, tachycardia, hepatomegaly)
Infection of the nidus (fever, local warmth)
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent referral.

b: Stabilisation: transfuse if severe anaemia, treat infection, optimise cardiac status.
Embolisation: use detachable coils or liquid embolic agents; preferred when DSA available.
Surgical resection: indicated for accessible, low‑grade lesions or after embolisation.
Medical adjuncts: anti‑epileptics for seizures; beta‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) for cutaneous AVM to reduce flow.
Avoid: systemic anticoagulation unless another indication, because it worsens bleeding risk.
sections.p: Treatment is staged: stabilise, control symptoms, then definitive nidus eradication when resources allow.

b: Clinic review every 6‑12 months with clinical exam and Doppler.
Repeat imaging (CTA/MRA) at 2‑year intervals for intracranial lesions.
Educate families on signs of rapid growth or bleeding.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and treat schistosomiasis to reduce hepatic AVM aggravation.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring detects recurrence and late cardiac effects.

b: Hemangioma – proliferative infant lesion, involutes spontaneously; lacks high‑flow shunt.
Arteriovenous fistula – single channel connection, usually post‑traumatic; AVM has a nidus.
Klippel‑Trenaunay syndrome – limb overgrowth with varicosities; AVM may be a component but not isolated.
sections.p: Conditions that also present with pulsatile masses or high‑output states.

b: Duplex ultrasound may miss deep nidus; negative study does not exclude intracranial AVM.
Normal CBC can coexist with occult bleeding; always correlate with clinical picture.
Early venous filling on CTA can be misread as normal venous phase if timing is off.
sections.p: Imaging and labs may give false reassurance.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden massive bleeding from the lesion
New onset seizure or focal neurological deficit
Signs of heart failure (tachycardia, dyspnoea, hepatomegaly)
Rapid increase in size with skin ulceration
